transcript.en: Mr Okafor and I each asked forty pupils about homework time. He found fifty minutes a day. I found sixty. Was one of us wrong? By the end, you'll be able to plan a fair school survey, and say how far its answer might be off. Think of a pot of soup. You taste one spoonful to judge it all. Stir it first, and any spoonful tells you the same. Taste only the top, and you may miss the salt at the bottom. The population is everyone the question is about: all four hundred pupils. The sample is the forty we actually ask. A random sample is the stirred spoonful: every pupil has the same chance. Pick forty pupils at random and you get one average. Pick another forty and you get a slightly different one. We took twenty random samples like this from the school records. Most land between fifty and sixty minutes, around the true value of fifty five. So we report a range, not one number. We say fifty five minutes, plus or minus five. That five is the margin of error. A bigger sample shrinks the margin, but four times as many pupils only halves it. Quick check! Another school asked five hundred pupils, all at its after-school club. That is far more than forty. Is its answer closer to the truth? Not for sure. A big sample can still be wrong if it is not random. If we only ask pupils who stay after school, we miss those who leave early to work. Always ask who was left out. Schools take samples all the time: one class in four for a reading check, or ten parents asked about a new timetable. A head count of every pupil is not a sample. It asks everyone, so there is no margin of error. In the app, open Samples and surveys. Set Pupils in each sample to ten, then to forty. Watch the typical wobble fall from about four minutes to under two. Then choose Only near the gate: every survey lands too low. Your turn. Mr Okafor found fifty minutes, and I found sixty, each from forty pupils picked at random. Was one of us wrong? No: random samples vary, so both answers can be honest. Remember: a random sample gives everyone the same chance. Report a range, with its margin of error. And ask who your sample left out. Try it in class tomorrow: put sixty numbered cards in a bag, and let each group draw ten and find the average. Write every group's average on the board and ask: why are they all different? Next lesson: finding groups that nobody has labelled.

body.en:
The population is everyone we care about, such as all 800 pupils; the sample is the group we actually ask. Different random samples give slightly different answers, so two honest surveys of 40 pupils can find 50 and 60 minutes of homework without either being wrong.

So report each result as a range: “50 minutes, plus or minus 5” and “60 minutes, plus or minus 5”. Both ranges include 55, so neither survey contradicts the other. That margin of error shrinks as the sample grows, but slowly: four times as many pupils only halves it. When you compare two groups, give each its range, and call the gap real only when the two ranges don’t overlap or touch.

Size is not enough. A sample must also be chosen fairly. Asking only the pupils who stay after school misses those who leave early to work, and asking a thousand of them would not fix it. Before trusting any survey, ask how the sample was chosen and who was left out.
body.ar:
المجتمع هو كل من يهمّنا، كجميع التلاميذ الـ ٨٠٠، والعينة هي المجموعة التي نسألها فعلًا. وتعطي العينات العشوائية المختلفة إجابات مختلفة قليلًا، فقد يجد استبيانان أمينان لـ ٤٠ تلميذًا ٥٠ و٦٠ دقيقة واجب دون أن يكون أيّهما مخطئًا.

لذلك اذكر كل نتيجة في صورة مدى: «٥٠ دقيقة، زائد أو ناقص ٥» و«٦٠ دقيقة، زائد أو ناقص ٥». ويضمّ المديان كلاهما ٥٥، فلا يناقض أحد الاستبيانين الآخر. ويصغر هامش الخطأ هذا كلما كبرت العينة، لكن ببطء: فأربعة أضعاف التلاميذ تنصّفه فقط. وحين تقارن مجموعتين، اذكر مدى كل منهما، ولا تعدّ الفرق حقيقيًا إلا إذا لم يتداخل المديان ولم يتلامسا.

والحجم لا يكفي. فيجب أيضًا اختيار العينة بعدل. فسؤال التلاميذ الذين يبقون بعد المدرسة وحدهم يفوّت من يغادرون مبكرًا للعمل، وسؤال ألف منهم لن يصلح ذلك. وقبل أن تثق بأي استبيان، اسأل كيف اختيرت العينة ومن تُرك خارجها.

transcript.en: I run the school library, so I keep its log. It shows how often each pupil borrows, and for how long. Nobody ever sorted these pupils into types. Could the numbers find groups by themselves? By the end, you'll be able to judge what groups found in data show, and give them names that harm nobody. Put each pupil on a chart: loans across, days kept up. No names, only dots. Yet the dots bunch into a few clouds. Finding those clouds without any labels is called clustering. Classification learns from examples that already have labels. Clustering has no labels at all. It looks for groups of cases that sit close together. The simplest method is called k-means. First choose k, the number of groups, and drop k centres anywhere. Each pupil joins the nearest centre. Then each centre moves to the middle of its pupils, and we repeat until nothing moves. Moving a centre is just finding a mean. The new centre's position is the average of its pupils' loans and the average of their days kept. That is the means in k-means. With k equal to three, the library pupils settled into three groups. Thirty pupils borrow often, forty borrow now and then, and twenty almost never. Quick check! Kofi lands in the group that almost never borrows. What does that tell us about Kofi? Only that his numbers look like theirs. Maybe he reads at home, or shares his brother's books. Calling a group lazy readers is our story, not the data's, and it can follow a child around. Clustering helps a school plan: which books to buy, or where to put a bus stop. Putting a new girl into one of our reading groups is not clustering: those groups already existed. In the app, open Find groups: the dots are houses, the rings bus stops. Press One step again and again, and watch the average walk shrink. Then set three stops and press New random start: the end can change. Your turn. Nobody ever sorted my library's pupils into types. Could the numbers find groups by themselves? Yes: pupils with similar numbers end up together, with no labels given. Remember: clustering finds groups without labels. k-means moves each centre to the mean of its group. And the names are ours, so choose them with care. Try it in class tomorrow: plot pupils' sleep and screen time without names, then let three pupils stand as centres. Everyone joins the nearest one, and the class works out where each centre should move. Next lesson: checking whether a tool is fair to every group.
transcript.ar: أنا مسؤول عن مكتبة المدرسة، فأنا اللي ماسك سجلّها. السجل بيبيّن كل تلميذ بيستعير قد إيه، وبيخلّي الكتاب معاه قد إيه. عمر ما حد قسّم التلاميذ دول لأنواع. يا ترى الأرقام تقدر تلاقي مجموعات لوحدها؟ في آخر الدرس، هتقدر تحكم المجموعات اللي بتطلع من البيانات بتقول إيه، وتدّيها أسامي متأذيش حد. حط كل تلميذ على رسم: الإعارات بالعرض، وأيام الاحتفاظ لفوق. من غير أسامي، نقط بس. وبرضه النقط بتتلم في كام سحابة. إنك تلاقي السحابات دي من غير أي تسميات اسمه التجميع. التصنيف بيتعلم من أمثلة عليها تسميات بالفعل. بس التجميع مفيهوش تسميات خالص. هو بيدوّر على مجموعات من الحالات قريبة من بعض. أبسط طريقة اسمها k-means. الأول اختار k، عدد المجموعات، وحط k مراكز في أي حتة. كل تلميذ بينضم لأقرب مركز. وبعدين كل مركز بيتنقل لوسط تلاميذه، ونكرر لحد ما مفيش حاجة تتحرك. تحريك المركز معناه بس إننا نحسب متوسط. ومكان المركز الجديد هو متوسط إعارات تلاميذه ومتوسط أيام احتفاظهم. ودي الـ means اللي في k-means: يعني المتوسطات. لما k بتلاتة، تلاميذ المكتبة استقروا في تلات مجموعات. تلاتين تلميذ بيستعيروا كتير، وأربعين بيستعيروا ساعات وساعات، وعشرين تقريبًا مبيستعيروش خالص. سؤال سريع! كوفي طلع في المجموعة اللي تقريبًا مبتستعيرش خالص. ده بيقولنا إيه عن كوفي؟ بس إن أرقامه شبه أرقامهم. ممكن بيقرا في البيت، أو بيشارك أخوه في كتبه. وإننا نسمّي مجموعة قرّاء كسالى دي حكايتنا إحنا، مش حكاية البيانات، وممكن تفضل ماشية ورا الطفل. التجميع بيساعد المدرسة تخطط: نشتري أنهي كتب، أو نحط موقف الباص فين. بس إننا نحط بنت جديدة في واحدة من مجموعات القراية بتاعتنا مش تجميع: المجموعات دي كانت موجودة قبل كده. في التطبيق، افتح «اكتشف المجموعات»: النقط بيوت، والدواير مواقف الباص. دوس «خطوة واحدة» مرة ورا مرة، وشوف «متوسط المشي» بيقصر. وبعدين خلّي المواقف تلاتة ودوس «بداية عشوائية جديدة»: النهاية ممكن تتغير. دورك. عمر ما حد قسّم تلاميذ المكتبة بتاعتي لأنواع. يا ترى الأرقام تقدر تلاقي مجموعات لوحدها؟ أيوه: التلاميذ اللي أرقامهم شبه بعض بيتلموا مع بعض، من غير ما حد يدّي تسميات. افتكر: التجميع بيلاقي مجموعات من غير تسميات. وk-means بتحرّك كل مركز لمتوسط مجموعته. والأسامي دي بتاعتنا إحنا، فاختارها بحرص. جرّبها في الفصل بكرة: ارسم ساعات النوم والشاشة للتلاميذ من غير أسامي، وخلّي تلات تلاميذ يقفوا مراكز. كل واحد ينضم لأقرب واحد، والفصل يحسب كل مركز المفروض يتنقل فين. الدرس الجاي: نتأكد الأداة عادلة مع كل مجموعة ولا لأ.
transcript.fr: Je dirige la bibliothèque de l’école, donc je tiens son registre. Il montre à quelle fréquence chaque élève emprunte, et pour combien de temps. Personne n’a jamais classé ces élèves par types. Les nombres pourraient-ils trouver des groupes tout seuls? À la fin, vous saurez juger ce que montrent des groupes trouvés dans des données, et leur donner des noms qui ne font de tort à personne. Placez chaque élève sur un graphique: les emprunts en largeur, les jours gardés en hauteur. Pas de noms, seulement des points. Pourtant, les points se regroupent en quelques nuages. Trouver ces nuages sans aucune étiquette s’appelle le regroupement. La classification apprend à partir d’exemples qui ont déjà des étiquettes. Le regroupement n’a aucune étiquette. Il cherche des groupes de cas proches les uns des autres. La méthode la plus simple s’appelle les k-moyennes. On choisit d’abord k, le nombre de groupes, et on pose k centres n’importe où. Chaque élève rejoint le centre le plus proche. Puis chaque centre se déplace au milieu de ses élèves, et on recommence jusqu’à ce que plus rien ne bouge. Déplacer un centre, c’est simplement calculer une moyenne. La nouvelle position du centre est la moyenne des emprunts de ses élèves et la moyenne de leurs jours de conservation. C’est le « moyennes » des k-moyennes. Avec k égal à trois, les élèves de la bibliothèque se sont répartis en trois groupes. Trente élèves empruntent souvent, quarante empruntent de temps en temps, et vingt presque jamais. Vérification rapide! Kofi tombe dans le groupe qui n’emprunte presque jamais. Que nous dit cela sur Kofi? Seulement que ses nombres ressemblent aux leurs. Il lit peut-être à la maison, ou partage les livres de son frère. Appeler un groupe « lecteurs paresseux » est notre histoire, pas celle des données, et elle peut suivre un enfant partout. Le regroupement aide une école à planifier: quels livres acheter, ou où mettre un arrêt de bus. Placer une nouvelle élève dans l’un de nos groupes de lecture n’est pas du regroupement: ces groupes existaient déjà. Dans l’appli, ouvrez Trouver des groupes: les points sont des maisons, les cercles des arrêts de bus. Appuyez encore et encore sur Une étape, et regardez la marche moyenne diminuer. Réglez ensuite trois arrêts et appuyez sur Nouveau départ au hasard: le résultat peut changer. À vous. Personne n’a jamais classé les élèves de ma bibliothèque par types. Les nombres pourraient-ils trouver des groupes tout seuls? Oui: les élèves aux nombres semblables se retrouvent ensemble, sans aucune étiquette donnée. Retenez: le regroupement trouve des groupes sans étiquettes. Les k-moyennes déplacent chaque centre vers la moyenne de son groupe. Et les noms sont les nôtres, alors choisissez-les avec soin. À essayer demain en classe: tracez le sommeil et le temps d’écran des élèves sans les noms, puis laissez trois élèves se placer comme centres. Chacun rejoint le plus proche, et la classe calcule où chaque centre doit se déplacer. Prochaine leçon: vérifier si un outil est équitable pour chaque groupe.
transcript.es: Dirijo la biblioteca de la escuela, así que llevo su registro. Muestra con qué frecuencia pide libros cada alumno y por cuánto tiempo. Nadie había clasificado nunca a estos alumnos por tipos. ¿Podrían los números encontrar grupos por sí solos? Al final, sabrás juzgar lo que muestran los grupos hallados en los datos y ponerles nombres que no dañen a nadie. Pon a cada alumno en un gráfico: los préstamos a lo ancho, los días que se queda con el libro hacia arriba. Sin nombres, solo puntos. Aun así, los puntos se juntan en unas pocas nubes. Hallar esas nubes sin ninguna etiqueta se llama agrupamiento. La clasificación aprende de ejemplos que ya tienen etiquetas. El agrupamiento no tiene etiquetas en absoluto. Busca grupos de casos que están cerca unos de otros. El método más simple se llama k-means. Primero elige k, el número de grupos, y coloca k centros en cualquier lugar. Cada alumno se une al centro más cercano. Luego cada centro se mueve al medio de sus alumnos, y repetimos hasta que nada se mueva. Mover un centro es simplemente calcular una media. La nueva posición del centro es el promedio de los préstamos de sus alumnos y el promedio de sus días de retención. Esa es la media de k-means. Con k igual a tres, los alumnos de la biblioteca se acomodaron en tres grupos. Treinta alumnos piden libros a menudo, cuarenta los piden de vez en cuando y veinte casi nunca. ¡Comprobación rápida! Kofi cae en el grupo que casi nunca pide libros prestados. ¿Qué nos dice eso de Kofi? Solo que sus números se parecen a los de ellos. Quizá lee en casa, o comparte los libros de su hermano. Llamar a un grupo «lectores perezosos» es nuestra historia, no la de los datos, y puede acompañar a un niño por mucho tiempo. El agrupamiento ayuda a una escuela a planificar: qué libros comprar, o dónde poner una parada de autobús. Poner a una alumna nueva en uno de nuestros grupos de lectura no es agrupamiento: esos grupos ya existían. En la app, abre Encontrar grupos: los puntos son casas y los círculos, paradas de autobús. Pulsa Un paso una y otra vez, y mira cómo se reduce el promedio de la caminata. Luego pon tres paradas y pulsa Nuevo inicio aleatorio: el resultado puede cambiar. Tu turno. Nadie había clasificado nunca a los alumnos de mi biblioteca por tipos. ¿Podrían los números encontrar grupos por sí solos? Sí: los alumnos con números parecidos acaban juntos, sin que nadie dé etiquetas. Recuerda: el agrupamiento encuentra grupos sin etiquetas. k-means mueve cada centro a la media de su grupo. Y los nombres son nuestros, así que elígelos con cuidado. Pruébalo mañana en clase: grafica el sueño y el tiempo de pantalla de los estudiantes sin nombres, y luego deja que tres estudiantes hagan de centros. Todos se unen al más cercano, y la clase calcula adónde debe moverse cada centro. En la próxima lección: comprobar si una herramienta es justa con cada grupo.
transcript.de: Ich leite die Schulbibliothek, also führe ich ihr Ausleihbuch. Es zeigt, wie oft jede Schülerin und jeder Schüler ausleiht und wie lange. Niemand hat diese Schüler:innen je in Typen eingeteilt. Könnten die Zahlen Gruppen von selbst finden? Am Ende kannst du beurteilen, was in Daten gefundene Gruppen zeigen, und ihnen Namen geben, die niemandem schaden. Trag jede Schülerin und jeden Schüler in ein Diagramm ein: Ausleihen nach rechts, behaltene Tage nach oben. Keine Namen, nur Punkte. Trotzdem ballen sich die Punkte zu ein paar Wolken. Diese Wolken ohne jedes Label zu finden, heißt Clustering. Klassifikation lernt aus Beispielen, die schon Etiketten haben. Clustering hat gar keine Etiketten. Es sucht nach Gruppen von Fällen, die nah beieinander liegen. Die einfachste Methode heißt k-Means. Wähle zuerst k, die Zahl der Gruppen, und setze k Zentren irgendwohin. Jede Schülerin und jeder Schüler schließt sich dem nächsten Zentrum an. Dann wandert jedes Zentrum in die Mitte seiner Gruppe, und wir wiederholen, bis sich nichts mehr bewegt. Ein Zentrum zu verschieben heißt nur, einen Mittelwert zu finden. Die neue Position des Zentrums ist der Durchschnitt der Ausleihen seiner Gruppe und der Durchschnitt ihrer Behaltetage. Das ist das Means in k-Means. Mit k gleich drei haben sich die Bibliotheksnutzenden in drei Gruppen eingependelt. Dreißig leihen oft aus, vierzig ab und zu und zwanzig fast nie. Kurzer Check! Kofi landet in der Gruppe, die fast nie ausleiht. Was sagt uns das über Kofi? Nur, dass seine Zahlen denen der anderen ähneln. Vielleicht liest er zu Hause oder teilt die Bücher seines Bruders. Eine Gruppe „faule Leser“ zu nennen ist unsere Geschichte, nicht die der Daten, und sie kann einem Kind nachlaufen. Clustering hilft einer Schule beim Planen: welche Bücher sie kauft oder wo eine Bushaltestelle hinkommt. Ein neues Mädchen in eine unserer Lesegruppen zu stecken, ist kein Clustering: Diese Gruppen gab es schon. Öffne in der App Gruppen finden: Die Punkte sind Häuser, die Ringe Bushaltestellen. Drück immer wieder auf Ein Schritt und sieh zu, wie der durchschnittliche Weg kürzer wird. Stell dann drei Haltestellen ein und drück auf Neuer Zufallsstart: Das Ende kann sich ändern. Jetzt bist du dran. Niemand hat die Schüler:innen meiner Bibliothek je in Typen eingeteilt. Könnten die Zahlen Gruppen von selbst finden? Ja: Schüler:innen mit ähnlichen Zahlen landen zusammen, ganz ohne Labels. Merk dir: Clustering findet Gruppen ohne Labels. k-Means setzt jedes Zentrum auf den Mittelwert seiner Gruppe. Und die Namen sind unsere, also wähle sie mit Sorgfalt. Probiere es morgen im Unterricht aus: Zeichne Schlaf und Bildschirmzeit der Lernenden ohne Namen ein, und lass drei Lernende als Zentren stehen. Alle schließen sich dem nächsten an, und die Klasse berechnet, wohin jedes Zentrum wandern soll. In der nächsten Lektion: prüfen, ob ein Werkzeug für jede Gruppe fair ist.

Chamar um grupo de leitores preguiçosos é uma história nossa, não dos dados, e isso pode acompanhar uma criança por muito tempo. O agrupamento ajuda a escola a planejar: quais livros comprar, ou onde pôr um ponto de ônibus. Colocar uma aluna nova em um dos nossos grupos de leitura não é agrupamento: esses grupos já existiam. Será que os números conseguem achar grupos sozinhos? Sim: alunos com números parecidos acabam juntos, sem nenhum rótulo dado. Lembre-se: o agrupamento encontra grupos sem rótulos. O k-means move cada centro para a média do seu grupo. E os nomes são nossos, então escolha-os com cuidado. Experimente em aula amanhã: marque no quadro o sono e o tempo de tela dos alunos, sem nomes, e depois peça a três alunos que sejam os centros. body.en:
Classification learns from examples that already have labels. Clustering has none: it looks for groups of cases that sit close together, such as pupils with similar library habits.

The k-means method is simple. Choose k, the number of groups, and place k centres. Each case joins its nearest centre. Each centre then moves to the mean of the cases that joined it. Repeat until nothing changes. Different starting centres or a different k can give different groups, so try a few and see which grouping is useful.

A cluster is a pattern of similar numbers, not a fact about a child. The names we give groups (“keen readers”, “reluctant readers”) are our interpretation, and a careless name can follow a pupil for years. Use clusters to plan support, such as which books to buy or which pupils to invite to a reading club, and never as a label on a record.

transcript.en: Our early-warning list flagged twenty girls and only five boys. A father asked me: is it unfair to girls? I had the list, and what really happened to each pupil. What should I count before I answer him? By the end, you'll be able to check whether a tool fails one group more, and whether the gap is real. An average can hide a group that a tool fails, as Audit an AI tool showed in the AI track. Here, we count it. Here is what really happened. Each group had twenty pupils who needed help and thirty who were fine. The tool caught seventeen of those girls, but only five of those boys. Now count each group's mistakes. The miss rate: of the pupils who needed help, the share it missed. The false alarm rate: of the pupils who were fine, the share it flagged. The error rate: of all its answers, the share that were wrong. So the girls' miss rate is three in twenty: fifteen percent. The boys' is fifteen in twenty: seventy five percent. Three fine girls were flagged too, a false alarm rate of ten percent. Is the gap real, or chance? Remember the margin of error: a rate from only twenty pupils can wobble by about twenty points. Sixty points is far bigger than that. Quick check! Another school's tool missed two of ten pupils in 7A, and three of ten in 7B. Is it unfair to 7B? Not yet. That gap is one pupil. A rate from ten pupils can wobble by about thirty points, so this could be chance. Count again next term. Count by group for any school tool: a reading app, a placement test, a marking rule. But before you publish an error rate, check the group's size. A rate for three pupils who use hearing aids points at named children. In the app, open Bias in data: a leaf-disease app. At five percent, it's wrong about three percent of the time overall. Yet it misses a third of the sick leaves in the hills. Drag the slider to fifty percent, and the regions come close. Your turn. The list flagged twenty girls and five boys. What should I count before I answer the father? Each group's misses and false alarms: here, the tool was failing the boys. Remember: count mistakes group by group. Check the gap against a small group's wobble. And publish no rate that points at a child. Try it in class tomorrow: give groups a made-up table of a tool's results for two classes. They work out each class's miss rate and decide whether the gap is real. Next lesson: deciding with a fair trial.

body.en:
A model is biased when its mistakes fall more on one group than another. The overall accuracy can look fine while one group, such as pupils with a village accent, girls, or pupils with a disability, carries most of the errors.

So split the test results by group and work out each group’s error rate. A big gap means the model is not fair to that group, whatever its average score. Also compare the kinds of mistake: a group may get more false alarms, or more misses.

Most bias starts in the data. If a reading app learned mainly from town voices, it will make more mistakes with other accents. Fixes include more varied training data, using the model only as a suggestion, and a person checking every important result. Before your school adopts any model, ask the supplier for its error rates by group, and test it on your own pupils.

transcript.en: Our staff wanted to move the start of the school day later. Some said pupils would sleep more and learn better. Others worried about parents' work. How could data help us decide? By the end, you'll be able to test a school change honestly, and plan who decides and how results are shared. We wrote one clear question: if we start thirty minutes later, will lateness and tiredness fall? Then we chose what to measure before collecting anything, so we could not pick the numbers we liked afterwards. Two classes started later for six weeks while two similar classes did not. Late arrivals per week fell from twelve to five in the trial classes, and barely changed in the others. That is a fair trial: try a change with some groups, and keep similar groups as they were. The similar classes are the comparison group. They show what would have happened anyway. The trial classes went from twelve to five: seven fewer late arrivals. The others went from eleven to ten: one fewer. So the effect of the later start is seven minus one: about six fewer a week. Quick check! Another school ran a reading club for a term, and marks rose by six. What should they ask before they say it worked? Did similar classes rise too? Marks often rise over a term anyway. If similar classes rose by four, the club's effect is only two. Fair trials fit many school questions: a reading club, a homework rule, a new timetable. A change tried in every class at once is not a fair trial. With no comparison group, it can't show an effect. Numbers were only half the story. We also asked parents and pupils, and some families could not manage the later finish. Their voices changed our plan more than any chart. In the app, open Decide with numbers. Under Weighted choice, set Cost to five and the rest to zero: the Farm wins. Then put Learning at five and Cost at zero: the Science centre wins. The scores never changed; what people value did. Your turn. Our staff argued about a later start. How could data help us decide? By showing the change's real effect, so people can weigh it with families' voices. Remember: fix the question and the measures first. Compare with a similar group: the difference is the effect. Then people decide, and share every result. transcript.fr: Notre équipe voulait repousser le début de la journée d’école. Certains disaient que les élèves dormiraient plus et apprendraient mieux. D’autres s’inquiétaient du travail des parents. Comment les données pouvaient-elles nous aider à décider? À la fin, vous saurez tester un changement d’école honnêtement, et prévoir qui décide et comment les résultats sont partagés. Nous avons écrit une question claire: si nous commençons trente minutes plus tard, les retards et la fatigue baisseront-ils? Puis nous avons choisi ce qu’il fallait mesurer avant de collecter quoi que ce soit, pour ne pas pouvoir choisir ensuite les chiffres qui nous plaisaient. Deux classes ont commencé plus tard pendant six semaines tandis que deux classes semblables ne l’ont pas fait. Les arrivées en retard par semaine sont passées de douze à cinq dans les classes de l’essai, et ont à peine changé dans les autres. Voilà un essai équitable: tester un changement avec certains groupes, et laisser des groupes semblables comme ils étaient. Les classes semblables sont le groupe de comparaison. Elles montrent ce qui se serait passé de toute façon. Les classes d’essai sont passées de douze à cinq: sept retards de moins. Les autres sont passées de onze à dix: un de moins. L’effet du démarrage plus tardif est donc sept moins un: environ six retards de moins par semaine. Vérification rapide! Une autre école a mené un club de lecture pendant un trimestre, et les notes ont monté de six points. Que doit-elle demander avant de dire que cela a marché? Des classes semblables ont-elles monté aussi? Les notes montent souvent au cours d’un trimestre de toute façon. Si des classes semblables ont monté de quatre, l’effet du club n’est que de deux. Les essais équitables conviennent à beaucoup de questions d’école: un club de lecture, une règle sur les devoirs, un nouvel emploi du temps. Un changement essayé dans toutes les classes à la fois n’est pas un essai équitable. Sans groupe de comparaison, il ne peut pas montrer d’effet. Les chiffres n’étaient que la moitié de l’histoire. Nous avons aussi interrogé les parents et les élèves, et certaines familles ne pouvaient pas gérer la fin plus tardive. Leurs voix ont changé notre plan plus que n’importe quel graphique. Dans l’appli, ouvrez Décider avec des nombres. Sous Choix pondéré, réglez Coût sur cinq et le reste sur zéro: la Ferme gagne. Mettez ensuite Apprentissage à cinq et Coût à zéro: le Centre scientifique gagne. Les scores n’ont jamais changé; ce que les gens valorisent, si. À vous. Notre équipe a débattu d’un démarrage plus tardif. Comment les données pouvaient-elles nous aider à décider? En montrant l’effet réel du changement, pour que chacun le pèse avec la voix des familles. Retenez: fixez d’abord la question et les mesures. Comparez avec un groupe semblable: la différence est l’effet. Ensuite, les gens décident, et partagent chaque résultat. À essayer avec votre équipe cette semaine: apportez une question de l’école à votre prochaine réunion et convenez de ce qu’il faut mesurer. Puis planifiez un petit essai, en gardant un groupe semblable inchangé pour une comparaison équitable. Ensuite: le bilan de l’unité.

body.en:
Data cannot make a school decision. It shows what is likely to happen and to whom, and people weigh what matters most. Good data-led decisions follow a few habits.

Start with one clear question and decide what to measure before collecting anything, so nobody can pick the numbers they like afterwards. Where you can, run a fair trial: try the change with some classes and keep similar classes as a comparison, because lateness or marks might change anyway with the season. The effect is the change in the trial group minus the change in the comparison group.

Listen as well as count. Surveys, interviews and complaints show costs that the numbers miss, such as families who cannot manage a later finish. Finally, share all the results, including what did not work. A regular data meeting where any teacher can bring a question builds a culture where small honest trials become how the school decides.

لا تستطيع البيانات اتّخاذ قرار مدرسي. فهي تُظهر ما قد يحدث ولمن، والناس يزنون ما يهمّ أكثر. وتتّبع القرارات الجيدة المبنية على البيانات عادات قليلة.

ابدأ بسؤال واحد واضح، وقرّر ما ستقيسه قبل جمع أيّ شيء، حتى لا ينتقي أحد الأرقام التي تعجبه بعد ذلك. وحيث يمكن، أجرِ تجربة عادلة: جرّب التغيير مع بعض الفصول واحتفظ بفصول مشابهة للمقارنة، لأن التأخير أو الدرجات قد تتغيّر على أيّ حال مع الموسم. والأثر هو التغيّر في مجموعة التجربة ناقص التغيّر في مجموعة المقارنة.

استمع إلى الناس ولا تكتفِ بالعدّ. فالاستبيانات والمقابلات والشكاوى تُظهر تكاليف تفوّتها الأرقام، كأسر لا تستطيع التعامل مع موعد انتهاء متأخر. وأخيرًا، شارك كل النتائج، ومنها ما لم ينجح. فالاجتماع المنتظم للبيانات، حيث يستطيع أيّ معلّم أن يأتي بسؤال، يبني ثقافة تصبح فيها التجارب الصغيرة الأمينة طريقة المدرسة في القرار.

en: Teams (2 min): Make teams of four and give each team a sheet for its answers.
Quiz (20 min): Read each question aloud; each team agrees on one answer and writes it down.
Explain (10 min): Reveal each answer and ask a team to explain it with an example from the unit.
Wrap-up (8 min): Work through the question most teams got wrong, together on the board.
